idiom_name: serialize-and-seal the conversation state into the request carrier (cookie, header or token)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: at the end of a request, serialize the conversation state into a compact, versioned blob, authenticate it with a MAC (and encrypt it when it holds anything sensitive), encode it (base64url) and write it to the carrier the client will return - a cookie, a custom header or an opaque token. At the start of the next request, read the carrier, verify the MAC (and decrypt) before parsing, reject stale or wrong-version records, and only then hand the deserialized state to the application as a session object. Application code must never see the carrier itself, and the reconstituted state must be treated as untrusted input even when the MAC verifies: integrity says who wrote the record, not that a client-supplied value is authorized.
code_sketch:
blob   = encode(state)                          # compact, versioned serialization
sealed = b64url(blob) + '.' + b64url(mac(blob))  # MAC first, encryption optional
response.set_carrier('sid', sealed, HttpOnly=True, Secure=True, SameSite='Lax', MaxAge=1800)

# next request
raw = request.carrier('sid')
session = Session.empty()
if raw and verify_mac(raw):                      # authenticate before parsing
    version, blob = decode_record(raw)
    if version in SUPPORTED and not stale(blob):
        session = deserialize(blob)              # still untrusted data
pitfalls: Read the carrier before the application runs and write the updated blob to the response after it runs; a handler that mutates state without the manager writing the new record silently loses the change on the next request.
The record is a snapshot: concurrent requests each start from their own copy, so the last writer wins unless the state is designed to merge or carries a version/etag that detects the conflict.
Authenticate before parsing - deserializing attacker-controlled bytes in order to inspect the MAC is the classic ordering mistake.

Algorithm confusion (alg:none / RS256-to-HS256): when the blob is a JWT, a verify function that accepts the token's declared alg to choose verification behavior can be exploited - an attacker crafts alg=HS256 and signs with the server's RSA public key as the HMAC secret, bypassing authentication entirely; always pin the algorithm explicitly (e.g., algorithms=['RS256']) and reject any token declaring an unexpected algorithm.

Size silent-failure: when the encoded blob exceeds the carrier's ceiling (4 KB per cookie), some clients truncate it; the server then receives a corrupted record it cannot distinguish from tampering; always check encoded size before shipping and fall back to server-side storage when the ceiling is neared.

Key confusion across instances: when using asymmetric keys, do not pass a public RSA key into a symmetric HMAC verification path; the same key material must not be used with two different algorithms in the same verification flow.

Wrong move: replacing a server-side session with a 24-hour stateless JWT to become stateless -> failure: logout, password change and role revocation all silently do nothing until the token ages out, and teams bolt on refresh tokens plus a revocation denylist, paying for both designs -> instead: either keep tokens genuinely short-lived (minutes) with revocable refresh tokens, or use a server-side session with an opaque id; do not pretend a long-lived JWT is a session.

Wrong move: embedding roles and permissions in the client-held token so authorization needs no lookup -> failure: a demoted or disabled user keeps stale privileges for the token's whole lifetime because the server never re-reads them -> instead: carry only identity in the blob and fetch current roles from the database or a fast cache per request, or bind them to a very short expiry.

Wrong move: treating the signed cookie as a private drawer -> failure: Play and Flask document that signing only proves authorship, so anything in a signed-but-not-encrypted cookie (PII, internal ids) is readable on the device and in any proxy or extension that can see the cookie -> instead: encrypt with an AEAD before signing, or keep the sensitive value server-side and put only a reference in the blob.
